# Background

## Pinot Noir is a key varietal for the Oregon wine industry

For many years, Burgundy, France was one of the only regions known for successful production of Pinot Noir. Among wine growers, Pinot Noir has a reputation as a difficult variety. It is thin-skinned and tightly clustered, it ripens early and is unusually sensitive to heat compared to more forgiving varieties like Cabernet Sauvignon or Merlot. For most of its history, Pinot Noir product was limited to regions like Burgundy that had a narrow band of warm, sunny days during the growing season paired with a pronounced overnight cooldown. These were the ideal conditions for the slow, gentle ripening required for great Pinot Noir.

In the 1960s, the winemaker David Lett set out to find a region outside of Burgundy that could sustain great Pinot Noir. He settled in Oregon's Willamette Valley, which sits on the same latitude as Burgundy (close to the 45th parallel) and shares many of the same climate characteristics [@napavalleywineacademy2025], including the day-night temperature swing that is vital to Pinot Noir's unique character. Lett entered his 1975 Eyrie Vineyards Pinot Noir in a blind tasting at the 1979 Gault-Millau French Wine Olympiad and placed among the top Burgandies. This was the first real signal that Oregon could compete at the same level as the region that had produced the best of the variety for over two thousand years [@kingestate2025].  The Willamette Valley became an official AVA in 1983 and has since become one of the most recognized Pinot Noir regions in the world, a status widely attributed to its warm-day, cool-night climate pattern [@oregonwine2025willamette; @sommselect2026].

# The diurnal range effect

This unique climate pattern is referred to as *diurnal temperature range*. Warm days drive photosynthesis and sugar accumulation in the grape. Cool nights slow the grape's respiration rate, which gives it time to retain the acids, color compounds, and aromatic molecules it built up during the day rather than burning through them overnight. Without this nightly cooldown, grapes ripen too fast and produce wines that taste "flat"—high in sugar without the balance of acidity and aromatic complexity that define great Pinot Noir [@ajev2012dtr; @kingestate2025].

An ideal diurnal range for Pinot Noir ripening is generally considered to be in the neighborhood of 15–20°C (~60-70°F). Controlled field and growth-chamber experiments on Pinot Noir, specifically, have shown that raising the diurnal temperature range around the onset of ripening (*véraison*) alters organic acid metabolism and can inhibit color and phenolic accumulation in the grape, with the size of the effect varying by season [@frontiers2025bunchheating]. While compression of the diurnal range has been shown to hasten ripening and shift how flavors develop in wine grapes broadly [@ajev2012dtr], targeted studies on Malbec, Merlot, and Pinot Noir have found that diurnal range sensitivity is not universal across varieties but is particularly pronounced in Pinot Noir [@pmc2022highTemp].

When we consider the impact of climate on wine production, particularly in Oregon where Pinot Noir is the dominant variety, it is not just a question of whether summers are getting hotter *overall*, but rather what happens when *nights warm faster than days*. This is a documented feature of twentieth- and twenty-first-century climate shifts globally, generally attributed to changes in cloud cover trapping heat overnight [@ucs2022nights; @liu2024dtr]. Section 4c of the [Analysis](#analysis) chapter shows that this is exactly the pattern we observe in the Oregon PRISM climate record: a real warming signal in growing degree days and heat stress, alongside a shrinking day-night swing during ripening. 

## Prior research on Oregon and Pinot Noir climate sensitivity

Climate research specific to Oregon wine has, to date, focused primarily on phenology and single-variety climate suitability rather than on production outcomes directly. Multi-decade climate analyses have documented measurable statewide warming, pushing the Willamette Valley from sitting at the cool edge of Pinot Noir suitability in the 1960-70s to sitting centered within that suitability range today [@jones2005]. Work presented at the Oregon Wine Symposium projects temperature-driven shifts in Oregon varietal suitability and harvest timing through 2100, pointing toward a potential reshuffling of the state's variety composition as the climate continues to warm [@skahill2025]. Separately, phenological modeling published in the *American Journal of Enology and Viticulture* has modeled shifts in Willamette Valley Pinot Noir's growth-stage timing, reinforcing the variety's particular sensitivity to the region's climate [@delelee2025]. 

We draw our general climate-threshold framework (growing degree days, frost days, heat stress days) from a global synthesis of viticulture climate impacts [@vanleeuwen2024]. This project differs from that body of work in one specific way: rather than modeling suitability or phenology on their own, we integrate 38 years of statewide production records directly with climate data to ask whether the warming trend has affected *production outcomes*, not just suitability. We then build a model that predicts yield from climate signals as they accumulate over the growing season.

## Filling an availability gap for Oregon wine data

Our motivation for this project is also driven by a genuine gap in publicly available data for Oregon wines. Due to the fact that 90% of U.S. wine grape acreage sits in California and Washington, USDA's National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) discontinued collecting Oregon-specific grape data beginning in 2011 [@nass2011gap]. While there was continued production and pricing data collection by researchers in Oregon, this information existed largely as scanned PDF reports rather than structured data. This project's data engineering work is built in part to close that gap: producing a structured, climate-linked Oregon wine dataset that does not currently exist from any single public source.
